list.listitem: The Amsterdam Pediatric Wrist Rule can be used to determine if further evaluation for a wrist fracture is indicated.B
The majority of wrist fractures are treated conservatively, with closed reduction and casting or splinting.B
The prognosis is generally good, and the majority of children have no long-term sequelae from a wrist fracture.C

background.definition: A wrist fracture is a disruption of one or more cortices of bone in the distal third of the ulna and radius, as well as the carpal bones. See for specific wrist fractures in children.

list.listitem: In the US population, there are 26 wrist fractures per 1000 children per year, with peaks at 14 years for males and 11 years for females.
Worldwide, wrist fractures represent 20% to 36% of all fractures in children. Overall, children have a risk of any fracture of 42% to 64% in males and 27% to 40% in females during childhood.
In the American high-school population, 8.5% of athletes sustained hand/wrist injuries (45% of which were fractures).
The average cost is $7000 per episode if seen in the emergency department; cases that require operative management can cost up to $24,000.
Forceful trauma, including falls, motor vehicle accidents, or sports activities (football, basketball, or soccer).
Children who are obese and sedentary are at higher risk of wrist fractures.

There are no obvious medically predisposing factors for wrist fracture. For example, there is no difference in baseline bone mineral density/content when comparing children with a first forearm fracture and those without.

The pediatric skeleton differs from an adult skeleton in that it has growth plates and proportionally more cartilage and collagen, which makes fractures more likely, though less likely to propagate. The fractures often occur in the transition zone between the dense lamellar bone of the diaphysis and the more porous metaphysis. This transition zone is more distal and closer to the physis in older children, and fractures can propagate into the physis.
Protective wrist splints have been found to reduce wrist injuries in sports such as snowboarding.C
Exercise can increase bone density levels and decrease risk of fracture.C

The physical exam, informed by the Amsterdam Pediatric Wrist Rules, can determine the need for imaging. Patients with one or more of the following should undergo x-ray: swelling of the distal radius, visible deformity, painful palpation of the distal radius, painful palpation at the anatomical snuffbox, or painful supination.B
Radiographs are often sufficient to diagnose fractures, although more advanced imaging may be required for more complex fractures.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Symptoms concerning for fracture without radiographic findings
Fall on outstretched hand, pain in anatomical snuffbox

list.listitem: Ask about the mechanism of injury (eg motor vehicle accident, sports, or fall on outstretched arm).

On inspection, wrist deformity is most specific. Findings with a high positive predictive value for wrist fracture include edema, pain on active or passive motion, pain on handgrip, and pain on supination.

Tenderness in the anatomic snuffbox, volar scaphoid tubercle, and thumb axial compression could indicate a scaphoid fracture; the sensitivity of these maneuvers combined was 100%, and the combined specificity was 74%.
A neurological exam should be performed to evaluate for possible nerve damage.
Distal pulses should be evaluated for possible compromise of circulation, which may occur in compartment syndrome.
Radiographs, including AP, lateral, and scaphoid views (if indicated), are first line. summarizes the abnormalities seen with different subtypes of wrist fracture in children.

Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) may be used to diagnose subtle scaphoid fractures if there is clinical suspicion without acute findings on radiograph. In a small prospective study with the examiner masked to the reference standard, the sensitivity was 100% and the specificity was 79%.

A trial randomized 270 children with a non-deformed distal forearm injury to initial POCUS or initial radiography. Compared with the final diagnosis established by an expert panel, a correct diagnosis was more often established in the initial POCUS group (98% vs 83%, p < 0.001). This was primarily due to better accuracy for buckle and "other" fractures.
POCUS is similarly accurate to radiographs for predicting adequacy of reduction of closed forearm fractures in children (LR+ 23, LR- 0.04).

A systematic review of ultrasound for elbow fractures found 8 studies with 880, approximately half of whom ultimately had a fracture. The pooled sensitivity was 97% and specificity was 90% (LR+ 9.8, LR- 0.03).
CT or MRI can better characterize severely comminuted fractures, although radiographs are usually sufficient.

The Amsterdam Pediatric Wrist Rule is useful for identifying patients who require further evaluation. If the patient has one of the following, radiography is indicated: swelling of the distal radius, visible deformity, painful palpation of the distal radius, painful palpation at the anatomical snuffbox, or painful supination. This rule has a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 37% (LR+ 1.5, LR- 0.1). It is therefore most helpful at ruling out fracture when negative.
See for a suggested approach to the patient.
Most fractures are managed conservatively, with reduction, then casting or splinting.B
POCUS is similarly accurate to radiographs for predicting adequacy of reduction of closed forearm fractures in children.
A subset of fractures, including open, Salter-Harris III to V, and displaced carpal fractures, require surgical management.C
There is no significant difference in pain control between groups of patients prescribed acetaminophen plus codeine versus ibuprofen.

Two randomized trials compared ibuprofen with ibuprofen + acetaminophen and ibuprofen + hydromorphone for children with acute musculoskeletal injury and found that ibuprofen alone was just as effective.
Indications for surgery include the following: Open fractures Salter-Harris grade III to V fractures Failure of closed reduction Failure of conservative therapy
Most fractures are managed conservatively, with reduction, then casting or splinting.
Studies have found that splinting and casting are similarly effective for distal radial, buckle and torus fractures in children.
POCUS is similarly accurate to radiographs for predicting adequacy of reduction of closed forearm fractures in children (LR+ 23, LR- 0.04).
Fractures of the ulnar styloid can co-occur with other fractures, generally thought to be of no consequence, even with non-union.
Removal of cast had similar outcomes whether done at home or in the clinic.

There is limited evidence from a Cochrane Review that surgical fixation with percutaneous wiring and cast immobilisation versus cast immobilisation alone after closed reduction of displaced fractures improves function and reduces treatment failure.

A review of 4867 pediatric forearm fractures at a pediatric tertiary care center found 33 fracture-related nerve injuries (0.7%). This included 19 ulnar, 8 median and 7 radial nerve injuries. Open fractures had a higher risk of nerve injury (9/53 or 17%).

Up to 34% of fractures re-displace. If re-manipulation is unsuccessful, operative management is required. Risk factors include increasing age, initial radial translation, ulna fracture, fracture to physis distance, and inadequate reduction.
Malunion of a fracture may require surgical correction.
Delayed union of a fracture is most commonly found after open reduction and may require surgical correction.
Compartment syndrome as a result of the injury or from operative management requires fasciotomy.
Nerve injury can be concomitant with the fracture or as a result of correction; most heal over time.
Scaphoid fractures may not be initially apparent and may require re-imaging.
See for definitions of specific fractures.

Buckle (torus) fracture: can be treated with a short arm cast or prefabricated splint for 4 to 6 weeks. In children with torus fractures of the distal radius, a randomized trial with 965 children with torus fracture of the distal radius found that soft bandages and rigid immobilization (with either a splint or a cast) are comparable with regard to pain, function, and quality of life. Complications only occurred in 1% in each group.
Greenstick fracture: minimally displaced greenstick fractures can be treated similarly to buckle fractures.

Complete fractures: splints are noninferior to casts in an isolated transverse radial fracture that is minimally angulated (<15°) and minimally displaced; splints have not been studied with both radial and ulnar fractures. Duration of therapy is similar to the buckle fracture.
Salter-Harris grade I to II: if non- or minimally displaced, Salter-Harris grade I to II fractures can be managed similarly to buckle fractures.

Closed, displaced, angulated fractures: radial and/or ulnar fractures with greater than 15° to 30° angulation (younger patients can tolerate greater angulation) will require a closed reduction prior to casting, with the general principles of traction, exaggerating the defect, and restoration of alignment. A below-elbow cast was found to be noninferior to an above-elbow cast for 4 to 6 weeks.
Open fractures: require operative management with reduction and internal fixation.
Closed, displaced, angulated fractures: if closed reduction or conservative therapy fails, may require surgical fixation. If the fracture is a carpal bone, it will require surgical fixation.
Salter-Harris grade III to V: may require surgical fixation, particularly if closed reduction does not achieve perfect alignment. Grade V fractures may not be apparent for months.
Children recover well and should regain the majority of function.C
Chronic sequelae can include continued pain, restricted mobility, and axial deviation.C
There is a temporary reduction of 5.6% (average) in bone mineral density during the recovery period, thought to be partly from immobilization. This is recovered 6 months after the injury.
Younger children (<5 years old) tend to have better outcomes.
Older age children (>10 years old) and healing with an angular deformity (greater than 20°) were both associated with poorer outcomes.
A majority (>70%) of patients do not have any long-term sequelae.
On long-term follow-up, forearm rotation was found to be restricted in up to 16% of patients. Only 2% of the population reported severe pain.
Regular follow-up for the first year after the injury should be arranged to monitor for growth arrest and/or a Salter-Harris type V fracture.

tr.td: Compression failure of the cortex without cortical disruption
Cortical disruption at the tension side of the fracture with intact cortex at the compression side
Disruption of both cortices (metaphysis and/or diaphysis). Fractures may be open where the bone is exposed and there may displacement and/or angulation present
Disruption of growth plate and metaphysis
Disruption of growth plate and epiphysis
Disruption of growth plate, metaphysis, and epiphysis
Crush injury of growth plate (may not be apparent initially)
